\title{Measuring Complex Tastes: A Multiple Factor Analysis of Preferences, Consumption, and Evaluations in Musical Taste}

\author{Omar Lizardo\\ \small University of California, Los Angeles} \date{October 2026}

\begin{document}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
\noindent This paper develops a way to measure complex tastes---cases where what people like, do, and praise do not line up---using data that record preferences, engagement, and evaluations of the same objects, whether genre categories or specific cultural items. The approach applies Multiple Factor Analysis (MFA), a Geometric Data Analysis (GDA) method, and lets us ask concrete questions about complex tastes: Do preference, engagement, and evaluation contribute equally to the structure that emerges? Do some dimensions of complex taste hang together more than others? The method also captures a duality: individuals vary in how much their own tastes are complex, and genres vary in how much they attract complex tastes from the people who encounter them. I demonstrate the approach using data on Americans' tastes in twenty musical genres, collected around 2012.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

Sociologists have measured cultural taste in at least three different ways \citep{ma2026tastes}. One tradition treats taste as \emph{preference}: a person's affective response to a cultural object. A second treats it as an orientation toward \emph{consumption}: actual participation or engagement in a cultural field. A third treats it as a faculty expressed in \emph{valuation}: judgments about the quality or status of cultural objects. Rather than resolving this ambiguity by fiat, \citet{ma2026tastes} argues that taste should be understood pluralistically, as a person's ``thick subjectivity'' in a cultural field---a multidimensional orientation expressed through the multiple aspects of action that guide our preferences, engagement, and evaluations.

Taking taste's multiple aspects seriously sharpens the idea of \emph{complex taste}. In simple tastes, the aspects agree: what a person likes, does, and values all point the same way. In complex tastes they do not: the guilty pleasure (liked and consumed but not valued), the taste pose (liked and valued but not consumed), distanced consumption (consumed but neither liked nor valued), and their kin \citep{ma2026tastes}.

This paper takes that pluralist conception seriously and builds a measurement strategy to match. The strategy applies Multiple Factor Analysis (MFA) \citep{pages2014mfa,abdi2013mfa}---a member of the Geometric Data Analysis (GDA) family that \citet{bourdieu1984distinction} used in his classic study \citep{rouanet2000geometric-a44, roux2004geometric-65c}---to a data structure in which each cultural object is described by three sets of indicators, one per aspect of taste. MFA's block structure lets us ask the questions the theory raises directly: How strong are the links between preference, consumption, and evaluation? Do the three aspects contribute equally to the shared structure of taste? And where, geometrically, do complex tastes live?

\section{Data and Measures}

\subsection{Data}

I use the Survey Sample International (SSI) 2012 Cultural Tastes Survey \citep{lizardo2012ssi}, a national sample of $N = 2{,}276$ American adults surveyed around 2012. For each of twenty musical genres, the survey measures how much a respondent likes the genre, whether they consume it, and how they perceive the social characteristics of its typical fans. Listwise deletion of the $17$ cases missing data on any of the $60$ analysis variables leaves an analytic sample of $N = 2{,}259$ respondents.

\subsection{Measures: Three Aspects of Taste for Twenty Genres}

Each genre contributes three binary indicators, one per aspect, for $20 \times 3 = 60$ variables organized into three blocks of twenty. \textit{Preference} comes from a four-point liking scale (like; dislike; neither like nor dislike; not familiar); a genre is coded $1$ if the respondent likes it and $0$ otherwise, treating unfamiliarity as non-liking on the reasoning that an affective response requires knowing the object. \textit{Consumption} (engagement) is whether the respondent checked having listened to the genre in the past month ($1 = $ listened, $0 = $ otherwise). \textit{Evaluation} comes from a check-all-that-apply list of the social characteristics respondents attribute to a genre's ``typical fan,'' so the categories are not mutually exclusive---a respondent can indicate both that the typical fan is a college graduate and that they did not attend college, or that they are both working class and upper class. A genre is coded $1$ if the respondent attributed \emph{unambiguously} high status to its typical fans---a college graduate without also indicating no college, \emph{or} middle or upper class without also indicating working or lower class---and $0$ otherwise.

Table~\ref{tab:genre-rates} reports how often respondents are coded $1$ on each indicator. Overall, $41.7\%$ of genre-responses are positive on preference, $22.9\%$ on consumption, and $20.7\%$ on evaluation. The unambiguous-status standard is demanding---it requires an uncontested high-status signal in at least one domain---so evaluation is the least frequently affirmed aspect: respondents grant a genre's fans unambiguous high status less readily than they like the genre or listen to it.

\section{Analytic Strategy}

Our data gives us three separate pictures of each person's taste: what they like, what they listen to, and what they think about the people who do. These three pictures might overlap heavily (a person who likes opera probably listens to it and sees its fans as high status), or they might diverge sharply (someone might listen to hip-hop while considering it low status). We need a method that asks: How much do these three pictures agree? Do they contribute equally to a single coherent picture of musical taste? And where, geometrically, do people end up when their three pictures don't line up?

Multiple Factor Analysis (MFA) \citep{pages2014mfa,abdi2013mfa} is built precisely for this kind of problem. It takes data organized into distinct blocks of variables---here, the three aspects of taste---and builds a single shared picture of the people while making sure no one block dominates. The MFA literature calls these variable sets ``groups''; we use \emph{blocks of variables}, or \emph{aspects} when referring specifically to preference, engagement, and evaluation, reserving ``group'' for its ordinary sociological meaning. In the geometric data analysis tradition, the distinct values a variable can take (here yes/no) are called \emph{categories}. The MFA approach proceeds in two steps, which we describe in the following sections. 

\subsection{Constructing the Global Complex Taste Space}

The raw data is a table with one row per respondent and sixty columns: twenty genres, each measured on three aspects. Each entry is binary, containing a 1 if the person likes/listens to/evaluates the genre highly, and 0 otherwise. 

\emph{Step 1: Analyze each aspect separately.} We run a separate analysis on just the liking data (20 genres, 2,259 respondents), treating it as a two-way table of yes/no responses. This analysis shows how respondents cluster by what they like. We repeat the process independently for listening and for evaluations. In technical terms, each of these is a Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA) on one block of twenty binary variables. The result of each separate MCA is a map of the respondents, showing who is similar to whom in terms of liking alone, listening alone, or evaluations alone.

\emph{Step 2: Balance and combine.} After the first step, the next step is to merge these three separate pictures into one. But we face a problem here because if one aspect naturally has stronger patterns than another (if listening, say, reveals much sharper clustering than evaluations), it will dominate the combined picture. To prevent this, we weight each aspect inversely to the strength of the first dimension of the separate MCA we just described. Specifically, we use the weights $5.00$ for preference, $6.45$ for consumption, and $4.28$ for evaluation. The intuition is like handicapping in golf: the aspect with the strongest internal structure gets downweighted so all three contribute equally to the final picture. The result is the ``complex taste space''---a single map of respondents where all three aspects are heard equally.\footnote{As a robustness check, we re-estimated the same MFA with each block analyzed by scaled PCA instead of MCA; the results hold. Eigenvalues, RV coefficients, and individual coordinates correlate at $r > 0.96$ across the first three dimensions. The main difference is how rare categories are weighted: MCA emphasizes rare (distinctive) answers, a feature we want here since unusual taste patterns carry theoretical interest.}

\subsection{Independence or Redundancy of Aspects of Complex Tastes}

Before we interpret the combined space, we need to answer a basic question: \emph{Are the three aspects empirically separate, or are they measuring the same thing in three different ways?} If they're measuring the same underlying thing, we could just use preference and ignore the others. If they're distinct, complex tastes can exist---and do exist---because people will occupy different positions in preference space versus listening space versus evaluation space.

The \textit{RV coefficient} measures this. It answers: ``How similarly do two aspects rank respondents relative to each other?'' If two aspects rank people identically (so whoever likes the most genres also listens to the most, and evaluates the most), the RV is 1. If they rank people completely independently (knowing whether someone likes a lot tells you nothing about whether they listen a lot), the RV is 0. RV runs from 0 to 1, and it's the multivariate analog of a correlation coefficient.\footnote{Formally, for each aspect $h$, the configuration matrix $\mathbf{S}_h$ captures pairwise respondent similarities based on that aspect's twenty variables. The RV coefficient between aspects $h$ and $k$ is the cosine of the angle between these two similarity structures: $\mathrm{RV}(h,k) = \mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_h \mathbf{S}_k) / \sqrt{\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_h^2)\,\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_k^2)}$. When a block has a single variable, RV reduces to the squared Pearson correlation.}

Now, if all three aspects were basically identical, we could measure complex tastes with just one of them. The fact that the RV coefficients are small---preference and consumption at $0.32$, and evaluation nearly unrelated to both at $0.01$ with each---tells us they're genuinely different. People who like many genres do tend to listen to many, but not overwhelmingly. And what people think about the fans? That's almost entirely separate from liking and listening. This independence is the geometric signature of the complex-taste idea: the three aspects are different enough that a person can like a genre without listening, listen without liking, and evaluate without either liking or listening.

\subsection{Participation of Each Aspect in the Global Space}

We've established that the three aspects are independent. But when we combine them, do all three actually contribute to the final picture, or does one get washed out? The \textit{$Lg$ coefficient} answers this question. It measures: ``How much of this aspect's own geometry survives in the combined picture?''

The $Lg$ coefficient ranges in a way that depends on the complexity of each aspect's structure. Because the balancing weights give each aspect equal influence at the start, the resulting $Lg$ values tell us whether each aspect leaves a detectable mark on the complex taste space. If one aspect had much weaker internal patterns, it could theoretically end up invisible in the combined picture despite starting with equal weight. Preference has an $Lg$ of $1.95$, consumption $2.48$, and evaluation $1.14$. All three are comparably strong, meaning all three aspects genuinely participate in structuring the complex taste space.\footnote{Formally, $Lg(h, \mathrm{MFA})$ is the inner product of the configuration matrix for aspect $h$ with the configuration matrix of the combined MFA, on an absolute scale. It measures participation in the compromise as a whole, not contribution to any single dimension.}

\subsection{Which Aspect Organizes Each Dimension?}

We know all three aspects participate in the space. But they don't participate equally on every dimension. The \textit{aspect contributions} answer: ``On this dimension, how much does each aspect contribute?'' On Dimension 1, is the pattern mostly about liking? Mostly listening? Or a balanced mix?

Contributions sum to $100\%$ per dimension, so we can ask: Does one aspect dominate this dimension, or do all three push together? The dimensions that are dominated by a single aspect are exactly where the aspects can come apart most sharply, and where complex tastes should be most visible. If Dimension 2 is $40\%$ preference, $50\%$ consumption, and $10\%$ evaluation, then evaluation is marginalized. But if Dimension 3 is $85\%$ evaluation and only $8\%$ each from preference and consumption, then that dimension is evaluation's own axis---a place where evaluations move independently of liking and listening.\footnote{The contribution of aspect $h$ to dimension $s$ is the sum of the squared coordinates of its twenty variables on that dimension, weighted and normalized by the dimension's overall variance.}

\subsection{Measuring How Much Individual Tastes Come Apart}

So far we've asked about the space as a whole: How independent are the aspects? Do all three participate? Which aspect owns which dimension? Now we flip to the individual level: \emph{For each person, on each dimension, how much do their three aspects agree?}

The technical machinery is this: Each person has three separate coordinates on Dimension 1---one based on their liking, one on their listening, one on their evaluations. Call these $F_{1,\text{preference}}$, $F_{1,\text{listening}}$, $F_{1,\text{evaluation}}$. Their global position on Dimension 1 is the average of these three. But the three might not be very close. Person A might have all three coordinates at $+2$ (strong agreement). Person B might have coordinates at $+3$, $+1$, and $-1$ (strong disagreement).

We measure this disagreement with a score $W_s(i)$. It captures: ``How spread out is this person's three partial coordinates around their average on this dimension?'' If all three are identical, $W_s(i) = 0$ (simple taste). If they're far apart, $W_s(i)$ is large (complex taste).

Mathematically, this decomposition holds exactly:
\begin{equation}
\sum_{h=1}^{H} F_{sh}(i)^2 \;=\; H \cdot F_s(i)^2 \;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{h=1}^{H} \left(F_{sh}(i) - F_s(i)\right)^2}_{W_s(i)},
\label{eq:decomp}
\end{equation}
where $F_s(i)$ is the person's global position and $W_s(i)$ is the disagreement score. The first term tells you where they sit; the second term tells you how much that position depends on which aspect you consult.

We can drill down further. The $W_s(i)$ score is made up of three pairwise disagreements: between liking and listening, between liking and evaluations, and between listening and evaluations. Each pairwise distance captures how far apart two aspects place a person on this dimension. The three pairwise distances sum exactly to $H \cdot W_s(i)$, so we can ask: ``Which pair of aspects is responsible for most of the disagreement?'' On Dimension 3 (status), the preference--evaluation and consumption--evaluation distances will likely be large (evaluations place people far from where liking/listening do). On Dimension 1 (engagement), they might be more balanced.\footnote{The squared pairwise distance between aspects $h$ and $k$ is simply $(F_{sh}(i) - F_{sk}(i))^2$. The three distances sum exactly to $H \cdot W_s(i)$ by algebra.}

An example makes the decomposition easier to grasp (Figure~\ref{fig:worked-example}). Consider a respondent who likes fifteen of the twenty genres---from jazz, Broadway/show tunes, and classic rock/oldies to top 40 and contemporary rock---listens to nine of them, and credits the fans of eighteen genres with unambiguously high status. On the first (horizontal) dimension, the general-affirmation axis, all three aspect points sit on the same side of the origin---preference at $+3.53$, consumption at $+3.05$, evaluation at $+2.28$, around a global point of $+2.95$---so the aspects disagree only about \emph{how much} this respondent engages, and only modestly: $W_1 = 0.8$, or 3\% of the projected partial inertia. The third (vertical) dimension, the status-valuation axis, tells a different story. The preference and consumption points sit slightly on the withholding side of the origin ($-0.66$ and $-1.33$), while the evaluation point lies far out on the side anchored by the genre evaluations ($+13.12$): this respondent grants high status to nearly every genre's fans, a generosity of valuation that far outruns both their liking and their listening. The global point is $+3.71$, and now the disagreement dwarfs the position: $W_3 = (-0.66 - 3.71)^2 + (-1.33 - 3.71)^2 + (13.12 - 3.71)^2 = 133.1$, or 76\% of the projected partial inertia---nearly everything that places this respondent on the status-valuation dimension is disagreement between aspects, not shared orientation.\footnote{In Ma's combinatorial terms (see Appendix~\ref{app:configurations}), the same respondent holds thirteen genres in complex configurations: one guilty pleasure, seven taste poses, four instances of distant praise, and one instance of distanced consumption.} The second dimension (right panel of Figure~\ref{fig:worked-example}) tells a third story for the same respondent: the preference point sits just on the popular side of the origin ($-0.89$), while consumption and evaluation sit on the highbrow side ($+1.74$ and $+4.31$), around a global point of $+1.72$, giving $W_2 = 13.5$---60\% of the projected partial inertia.\footnote{As the discrete complement to this geometric measure, each genre--respondent pair is classified into one of Ma's eight configurations from the binary triple of orientations (preference, consumption, evaluation): the simple taste $(+++)$, the simple non-taste $(---)$, and the six complex tastes (Appendix~\ref{app:configurations}).}

\centering
\includegraphics[width=.9\linewidth]{fig-worked-example} \caption{\footnotesize Worked example: partial points of one respondent, shown against the status-valuation axis (Dimension 3). The left panel pairs it with the general-affirmation axis (Dimension 1), the right panel with the highbrow--popular axis (Dimension 2). Colored points are the aspect-specific partial points; the black diamond is the respondent's global (compromise) position, their average. In the left panel, the sum of squared horizontal deviations from the compromise is $W_1 = 0.8$ (3\% of the projected partial inertia) and the sum of squared vertical deviations is $W_3 = 133.1$ (76\%); in the right panel, the horizontal deviations give $W_2 = 13.5$ (60\%).}

\section{Results}

\subsection{Overall Structure of the Complex Taste Space}

How large and clear are the patterns in the complex taste space? Table~\ref{tab:eigen} shows that the first dimension captures $9.6\%$ of the variation, the second $7.5\%$, and the first five dimensions together $32.5\%$. These percentages are typical for data like ours---binary yes/no responses scattered across twenty genres. Much of the variation is genre-specific (whether you like opera has little to do with whether you like hip-hop), so no single dimension captures huge amounts.\footnote{We conducted all analyses in \textsf{R} using \textsf{FactoMineR}; scripts reproducing all results are available in the replication materials.}

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering \caption{Eigenvalues of the MFA (first five dimensions).}
\label{tab:eigen}
\input{tables/tab-eigen}
\end{table}

The category coordinates reveal what each dimension means. On the first dimension, the pattern is simple and strong: the yes categories of preference and consumption (especially the rarest ones---folk at $+1.43$, bluegrass at $+1.34$) sit on the positive side; the no categories sit on the negative side. Status attributions barely move along this dimension (ranging from $+0.03$ for Broadway to $+0.53$ for rap). This is the \emph{engagement volume} dimension---where people sit depends on how many genres they like and listen to, regardless of what they think of the fans. Respondents who like and listen to many genres sit on the positive side. Those who like and listen to few sit on the negative side. Evaluations are nearly silent here, saved for Dimension 3.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=.85\linewidth]{fig-categories} \caption{Category map of the MFA (dimensions 1--2). Colored points are the ``yes'' categories of each aspect; grey points are the corresponding ``no'' categories. Preference and consumption ``yes'' categories array along the positive side of Dimension 1 (general affirmation); the evaluation ``yes'' categories barely spread along it, while splitting highbrow (top) from popular (bottom) on Dimension 2.}
\label{fig:categories1-2}
\end{figure}

Dimension 2 cuts across genres along a hierarchical line. The highbrow genres (opera, classical, big band, Broadway) sit at the positive pole, while popular genres (rap, heavy metal, indie, dance/club, reggae) sit at the negative pole. Strikingly, this opposition shows up identically across all three aspects. Whether you measure liking, listening, or evaluations, the same genres cluster together. This is the classic \emph{highbrow--popular hierarchy} that researchers have documented for decades \citep{bourdieu1984distinction}. Respondents move along this axis depending on where they fall in that genre hierarchy---older people tend toward highbrow (Section~\ref{sec:social}), younger toward popular.

The vertical axis of the category map (Dimension 3) tells a different story. All twenty evaluation yes categories sit clustered on the positive side of the origin. The preference and consumption yes categories, by contrast, are scattered all around zero. This is the \emph{status-valuation} dimension---it's almost entirely evaluation's axis. A respondent's position here depends almost solely on whether and how much they grant high status to genres' fans, independent of their liking or listening.

\subsection{Independence or Redundancy Among Complex Taste Aspects}

The Analytic Strategy section asked: Are the three aspects distinct or the same thing measured three ways? The RV coefficients answer the question empirically. Preference and consumption rank respondents quite similarly (RV = 0.32), but not identically. If you like a lot of genres, you probably listen to a lot too. But not everyone who listens a lot likes a lot, and vice versa---the two are far from perfectly correlated.

Evaluation, though, is a different story. It shows an RV of $0.01$ with both preference and consumption. This near-zero is the key empirical finding: evaluations rank respondents almost completely independently of their liking and listening. Knowing whether someone likes many genres tells you virtually nothing about whether they grant high status to genres' fans. The three aspects are genuinely distinct. What you like, what you listen to, and what you praise are three separable dimensions of taste. This is why complex tastes exist: a person can like a genre without listening to it, listen without liking, or evaluate highly without either liking or listening. None of these patterns is surprising or contradictory. They're the natural result of the three aspects being structurally independent.

\subsection{How Each Aspect Participates in Each Dimension}

We've seen that all three aspects contribute to the global space. But they don't contribute equally to every dimension. On Dimension 1 (engagement volume), liking and listening align perfectly (correlations $0.84$ and $0.86$ between their separate axes and the global axis). Evaluations barely correlate with this dimension ($0.19$). On Dimension 2 (highbrow--popular), liking and listening again dominate, with the genre hierarchy showing up consistently in both. Evaluations contribute only modestly ($0.35$ correlation). But Dimension 3 is evaluation's own axis: it correlates almost perfectly with evaluation's separate structure ($0.91$) and hardly at all with preference and consumption.

What this means: The first two dimensions are genuinely shared. All three aspects place people along the engagement and hierarchy axes in ways that correspond to each other. The third dimension, though, is special. It's almost entirely driven by evaluations. Preference and consumption barely vary along it. Respondents' liking and listening tell you almost nothing about where they sit on the status-valuation dimension. That's determined almost purely by their evaluations.

\subsection{Which Aspect Dominates Each Dimension?}
\label{sec:contrib}

We've seen that dimensions 1 and 2 are shared across aspects, while dimension 3 is evaluation-dominated. But how dominant is each aspect on each dimension? On Dimension 1, is the split 50-50-0, or more balanced? We can answer this by looking at the aspect contributions---the percentage of each dimension's variation that comes from each aspect. Table~\ref{tab:groups} shows these percentages alongside the $Lg$ coefficients, which measure overall participation.

\label{tab:groups}

\end{table}

\centering \caption{Partial axes: correlations between each aspect's separate-analysis axes and the first three MFA dimensions.}
\label{tab:partial-axes}
\input{tables/tab-partial-axes}
\end{table}

The pattern is clear: Dimensions 1 and 2 are genuinely shared. Preference and consumption contribute roughly equally to both (around 48\% each on Dimension 1, 40--49\% on Dimension 2), while evaluation contributes modestly (2.5\% and 11\%). But Dimension 3 breaks the pattern entirely. Evaluation accounts for 83.9\% of it, while preference and consumption each contribute only 8\%. 

This reflects the fundamental structure of the space. Respondents' liking and listening reveal which rung of the genre hierarchy they occupy. But their evaluations reveal something else: how far down the hierarchy they're willing to extend recognition. The evaluation yes categories are ordered by rarity---granting status to rap fans is a distinctive move ($+1.87$), while granting it to opera fans is nearly universal ($+0.20$) and barely differentiates respondents at all. Dimension 3 is thus evaluation's own axis, where preference and consumption barely vary.

\subsection{Measuring Complex Tastes}
\label{sec:antinomies}

Now we get to the core question: \emph{For each person, on each dimension, how much do their three aspects disagree?} We measure this with the score $W_s(i)$ (Equation~\ref{eq:decomp}), the dispersion of a person's three partial coordinates around their global position. It's zero when all three aspects place them at the same location (simple taste) and grows as they place them further apart (complex taste).

What's surprising is how much complex tastes matter geometrically. On Dimension 1, the disagreement score accounts for 56\% of respondents' variation on that dimension. On Dimension 2, it's 52\%. On Dimension 3, it's 63\%. This means disagreement is about as important as agreement in determining where respondents sit in the space. Complex tastes aren't a marginal phenomenon confined to a few unusual respondents. They're woven throughout the structure of the space.

We can also count complex tastes combinatorially: How many of a person's 20 genres fall into each of Ma's eight configurations? (Appendix~\ref{app:configurations} defines these.) The geometric and combinatorial measures are related but different. The geometric score on Dimension 1 correlates with the combinatorial count ($\rho = 0.31$), but on Dimensions 2 and 3 the correlation is much weaker ($0.19$ and $-0.06$). The reason: The geometric score measures \emph{how much} the aspects disagree on this dimension; the configuration count measures \emph{how many genres} a person holds in each configuration. They align on engagement (Dimension 1) but diverge on position (Dimension 2) and evaluation (Dimension 3).

Each configuration type also has its own signature in the space. Distant praise---liking and evaluating highly but not listening---sits at the status-granting pole of Dimension 3, concentrated in prestige genres like opera. Guilty pleasures---liking and listening but not evaluating---sit at the popular and status-withholding poles (Dimensions 2 and 3), where genres like classic rock sit. Taste poses---liking and evaluating but not listening---sit toward the highbrow and engaged end of the space. The eight configurations form a consistent map of where complex tastes cluster geometrically.

\subsection{The Social Sources of Complex Tastes}
\label{sec:social}

A key question: \emph{Is complex taste concentrated in certain demographic groups, or scattered across society?} We can project respondent demographics (age, education, class, race, gender, region) onto the MFA space to see which groups sit where and how strongly demographics predict each dimension's positions. We do this ``after the fact''---these variables don't influence the analysis itself, just map onto the finished space. The strength of association is measured by $\eta^2$, a statistic ranging from 0 (no association) to 1 (perfect prediction).

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering \caption{Correlation ratios ($\eta^2$) between supplementary demographic variables and the first four MFA dimensions.}
\label{tab:eta}

\end{table}

\end{table}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig-supplementary} \caption{Supplementary demographic category barycenters (dimensions 2--3). Axis range covers the category coordinates only.}
\label{fig:supplementary}
\end{figure}

The highbrow--popular dimension (Dimension 2) is heavily shaped by age and education. Age is the strongest anchor ($\eta^2 = 0.33$): 18--29-year-olds sit at the popular pole ($-0.74$), while those 70+ sit at the highbrow pole ($+1.23$). Education follows the same gradient: those without a diploma sit toward popular ($-0.26$), those with graduate degrees toward highbrow ($+0.67$). Subjective class also matters: those who identify as upper class sit toward highbrow ($+0.39$), those as lower class toward popular ($-0.35$). The genre hierarchy is thus a social hierarchy. What you listen to correlates closely with your age and education.

The general-affirmation dimension is only weakly socially structured---no demographic variable exceeds $\eta^2 = 0.03$ on it---but the education pattern is instructive: the gradient concentrates at the bottom of the credential distribution (No diploma $-0.39$, HS/GED $-0.24$) and flattens from some college upward ($+0.05$ to $+0.13$). Generalized engagement with the genre system, in other words, is most sharply differentiated at the entry into credentials, not across their full range.

Dimension 3 (status-valuation), by contrast, is \emph{socially flat}. No demographic variable predicts it ($\eta^2$ all below 0.011). All demographic groups cluster near the center, regardless of age, education, or class. Who grants status to genres' fans isn't predicted by who you are demographically. This fits what we learned earlier: evaluations are nearly independent of liking and listening (RV = 0.01). The status-valuation axis isn't a demographic gradient at all. It's structured by something else entirely---perhaps individual-level variation in the willingness to recognize different forms of cultural engagement.

\subsection{Who Has Complex Tastes?}
\label{sec:who}

We've shown that complex tastes are geometrically important and spread throughout the space. But are they concentrated in particular demographic groups? If younger people have more complex tastes, or if they're concentrated among the college-educated, that would matter for understanding the phenomenon.

The answer is surprising: \emph{they're scattered across all demographic groups}. Table~\ref{tab:regression} shows OLS regressions of each $W_s$ score on the eight demographics. The results are telling: demographics explain only $5.2\%$ of the variation in $W_1$, $2.0\%$ in $W_2$, and $2.1\%$ in $W_3$. By contrast, where you sit in the space (your global position on each dimension) is strongly predicted by demographics ($\eta^2$ ranging from 0.03 to 0.33). You can predict fairly well whether someone likes highbrow or popular music based on their age and education. But predicting how much their liking, listening, and evaluating disagree? Much harder. Complex tastes aren't the signature of any one social location.

The few effects that do appear are minor. On $W_1$ (engagement disagreement), those with college-educated parents and those who identify as upper class score slightly higher. On $W_2$ (hierarchy disagreement), only age matters slightly. On $W_3$ (status disagreement), upper-class identifiers score noticeably higher. If anything, complex tastes are slightly more common among the educated and affluent. But the overall pattern is clear: complex tastes are a general feature of individual taste profiles, not concentrated in any social group. The three aspects---liking, listening, evaluating---are weakly coupled for everyone, not just for certain demographic groups. The disagreement between them is as likely to appear among young people and working-class respondents as among older people and the college-educated.

\subsection{The Duality: Genres as Targets of Complex Tastes}
\label{sec:duality}

Complex tastes have a dual structure: individuals are \emph{sources} of complex tastes, and genres are \emph{targets}. Which genres attract complex tastes? Some genres (like opera) elicit unified responses: most people's liking, listening, and evaluation all point the same direction. Others split people.

To answer this, we flip the analysis: rows become genres, columns become respondents, measured on their liking, listening, and evaluations of each genre. We re-run the MFA with genres as units. This reveals how genres distribute across the complex taste landscape. Note that dropping respondents with constant values (always like/listen/evaluate or never do so), we exclude 83, 84, and 326 respondent-variables respectively. The transposition is not a mere rearrangement of the original solution. In simple correspondence analysis, the row and column clouds are dual, so genre coordinates could be read off the original fit at no cost; but multiple correspondence analysis with a block structure breaks that duality. The original analysis's category coordinates locate a genre through the composition of its audience---the barycenter of the respondents who affirm it---while the transposed analysis locates genres as objects, with distances computed over the respondent-indicators within each aspect block. Because MFA weights each block by the inverse of its separate analysis's first eigenvalue, and transposing changes the separate analyses, the balancing weights and hence the eigen-decomposition differ: the transposed dimensions are optimized for the dispersion of the genre cloud rather than the respondent cloud ($\lambda_1 = 2.27$ here against $1.51$ above). And statistics defined over the individuals of an analysis---RV coefficients and partial points among them---don't survive transposition: the genre-level RV coefficients and aspect-specific genre partial points reported below exist only in the transposed fit. The transposed MFA was implemented by direct application of the algorithm in \citet{pages2014mfa} and validated by reproducing the respondent-level \textsf{FactoMineR} solution: eigenvalues, global and partial coordinates, RV coefficients, and group contributions all agree to within $10^{-4}$.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig-genre-map} \caption{Genre map from the transposed MFA. Black points: genre compromise positions; colored points: aspect partial points (segments connect each genre's compromise to its aspect-specific positions).}
\label{fig:genre-map}
\end{figure}

Here's the surprise: From the genre perspective, the aspects \emph{agree} strongly. The RV coefficients are $0.92$ (preference--consumption agree), $0.53$ (preference--evaluation), and $0.49$ (consumption--evaluation)---far higher than the individual-level $0.32$, $0.01$, and $0.01$. People who like a genre tend to listen to it and grant its fans status. But this doesn't contradict our individual-level findings. The agreement is \emph{at the aggregate level}. Yes, the liking population and the listening population overlap substantially for each genre. But \emph{which individuals} occupy which positions varies. Complex tastes aren't a property of genres; they're a property of individuals. One person's complex taste is another person's simple taste.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering \caption{Genre target profiles: percentage of respondents holding each genre in each of Ma's configurations ($N = 2{,}259$).}
\label{tab:genre-profile}
\input{tables/tab-genre-profile}
\end{table}

The transposed space is itself strongly structured ($\lambda_1 = 2.27$, $14.6\%$ of the inertia; $\lambda_2 = 1.95$, $12.5\%$). Its second dimension is a \emph{configuration axis}: genres are ordered by the complex-taste profiles they attract (Table~\ref{tab:genre-profile}). At the positive pole sit the genres respondents actively hold---in simple positive taste ($\rho = +0.77$), as taste poses ($+0.55$), as guilty pleasures ($+0.44$), or as justified abstentions ($+0.44$)---led by classic rock/oldies ($+3.7$), mood/easy listening ($+2.0$), country ($+1.8$), and top 40/pop ($+1.3$). At the negative pole sit genres whose dominant relation is simple non-taste ($\rho = -0.73$): rap/hip-hop ($-1.7$), reggae ($-1.5$), Latin/Spanish/Salsa ($-1.3$), and heavy metal ($-1.3$)---together with opera ($-1.2$), whose relation to its audience is instead dominated by distant praise ($58.9\%$ of respondents hold it in that configuration). The duality is asymmetric in exactly the way complex-taste theory anticipates: the prototypical guilty-pleasure genres are among the least credited with high status (evaluation rates of $8$--$14\%$ for classic rock/oldies, country, and top 40), and the prototypical distant-praise genre is the least consumed ($8.5\%$ for opera). The first dimension opposes genres whose typical relation is status without engagement---classical ($-3.6$), opera ($-3.0$), and Broadway/show tunes ($-2.1$), with distant-praise rates loading at $-0.82$ and taste-pose rates at $-0.58$---against genres held in guilty pleasure ($\rho = +0.75$) and distanced consumption ($+0.80$): top 40 ($+2.0$), rap/hip-hop ($+1.8$), classic rock/oldies ($+1.3$), and contemporary rock ($+1.3$)---familiar genres most often held with engaged disagreement.

Finally, the partial points show where the aspects disagree about specific objects despite their overall agreement. On the third dimension, the evaluation partial points of consecrated genres sit displaced toward positive values relative to their preference and consumption partial points (classical: $+2.3$ for evaluation against $+1.0$ for preference and $+0.9$ for consumption; opera: $+2.3$ against $-0.0$ and $+0.1$), while country shows the reverse displacement (evaluation $-0.8$ against $-3.1$ and $-4.1$). Status attributions, in other words, are distributed across genres in a way that only partially tracks who likes and who listens---echoing, at the level of objects, the aspect independence we already established at the level of sources.

\section{Discussion}

\section{Discussion}

This paper has pursued a geometric approach to measuring complex tastes---the misalignments between preference, consumption, and evaluation in cultural fields. The results support three core findings about musical taste in contemporary America.

\emph{First, the three aspects are empirically independent.} Preference and consumption correlate moderately (RV = 0.32), but evaluation is nearly orthogonal to both (RV = 0.01). This independence is the geometric signature of the complex-taste concept. If all three were measuring the same underlying thing, we could ignore two of them. But they don't. What you like, what you listen to, and what you praise are three separable judgments that follow different logics.

\emph{Second, the shared structure is primarily two-dimensional.} The first dimension is engagement volume: how many genres someone likes and listens to. The second is the classical highbrow--popular hierarchy. Both dimensions are visible across all three aspects, reflecting shared cultural structures that shape how people organize musical taste. Evaluations are largely silent on these dimensions, appearing only modestly on the first and second, but dominating a distinct third dimension.

\emph{Third, complex tastes are ubiquitous.} The disagreement scores ($W_s$) account for $56\%$, $52\%$, and $63\%$ of variation on the three dimensions. Combinatorially, the average respondent holds $10.2$ of $20$ genres in complex configurations. Only 12 respondents (of 2,259) hold no complex configuration at all. This is not a marginal phenomenon. Complex tastes are woven throughout the taste landscape.

A surprising finding follows: complex tastes are not concentrated in any social group. Where respondents sit (whether they prefer highbrow or popular genres) is strongly predicted by age, education, and class. But how much their three aspects disagree is nearly unpredictable from demographics. The dispersion that makes a person's taste complex is orthogonal to the social positions that sort people by consumption patterns. This fits the individual-level theory. The independence of the aspects at the population level generates disagreement at the individual level whenever people don't occupy all three positions simultaneously.

Finally, the duality reveals something crucial: from the genre perspective, the aspects agree. Liking, listening, and evaluation audiences overlap substantially. But because individuals don't equally participate in all three audiences, complex tastes emerge. A person may be a genuine opera enthusiast (likes, listens, praises) or a genuinely uninterested person (none of the above) or any combination. The eight configurations are not rare types; they're how ordinary people relate to culture when three incompletely correlated judgment systems structure their engagement.

Future work might explore whether these patterns generalize to other cultural fields---visual art, film, fashion---or whether music has distinctive properties. The geometric approach makes possible precise measurement of the degree to which cultural judgment is unified or fragmented. The results here suggest it's fundamentally fragmented.

\appendix

\section{The Combinatorial Measure: Ma's Eight Configurations}
\label{app:configurations}

The geometric measure locates complex tastes continuously in the common space. As a discrete complement, each genre--respondent pair can be classified into one of Ma's eight configurations from the binary triple of orientations (preference, consumption, evaluation): the simple taste $(+++)$, the simple non-taste $(---)$, and the six complex configurations.

Complex tastes are the statistical norm of this taste culture, not the exception. Figure~\ref{fig:configurations} reports the mean number of genres held in each configuration: the average respondent holds $10.2$ of the $20$ genres in a complex configuration, and only $12$ of $2{,}259$ respondents hold no complex configuration at all. The most frequent complex configuration is the \emph{justified abstention} ($3.3$ genres on average), followed by the \emph{guilty pleasure} ($3.2$) and \emph{distant praise} ($2.2$): respondents routinely like genres whose fans they don't credit with high status, grant high status to genres they neither like nor consume, and like-and-consume genres whose fans they don't credit that way. The taste pose ($1.0$) and the rare variants---distanced consumption ($0.4$) and the pre-acquired taste ($0.1$)---are comparatively infrequent, while the simple non-taste ($8.9$) is the single largest configuration.
